reason: Vision language models face a fundamental geometry trade-off: Euclidean representations excel at instance-level discrimination, while hyperbolic representations naturally encode semantic hierarchies. Hybrid training is challenging because one geometry may dominate early, leaving the other under-trained failure mode we term geometry dominance. We introduce Adaptive Geometry Routing (AGR), a framework that addresses this via a novel four-phase training curriculum : (1) Isolation hyperbolic-only training stabilizes hierarchical structure; (2) Shadow router learns mixing patterns using only hyperbolic signals; (3) Soft Launch Euclidean scores gradually become visible; (4) Adaptive full dual-geometry routing. This phased coordination of router activation (?) and Euclidean visibility (?) prevents early dominance while enabling data-driven geometry selection. Built on a shared backbone with lightweight LoRA-adapted heads and bounded residual corrections, AGR discovers that hyperbolic geometry is preferred by default (85% weight), with routing adapting semantically abstract queries route more hyperbolic, attribute-rich queries shift toward Euclidean. On ViT-B, AGR achieves 38.8% COCO T2I R@5 (+6.5pp over MERU), 64.7% Flickr30K I2T R@5 (+11.3pp), and 32.6% ImageNet accuracy (+9.3pp), demonstrating that phased curriculum training enables stable hybrid geometry learning for vision-language understanding.
title: Adaptive Geometry Routing for Vision-Language Understanding
